title: What is money
explanation:
Open your wallet and look at a ₹100 note. It is just paper with ink on it — you cannot eat it or wear it. Yet the auto driver accepts it, BigBasket accepts it, and your landlord accepts it. Money works because everyone agrees it has value.

In India, the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) prints rupees and manages the banking system. When you get salary via NEFT or pay with UPI, you are using that shared system. You are not trusting one shopkeeper — you are trusting a whole country-wide agreement.

The tricky part: a rupee does not stay equally powerful forever. A vada pav that cost ₹15 ten years ago might cost ₹30 today. So money is not just about having notes — it is about what those notes can actually buy for you.

title: Compounding
explanation:
Imagine you plant one mango seed. Next year you get fruit, and some seeds fall and grow into more trees. Compounding is the same idea with money — you earn returns, and then those returns start earning returns too.

The magic is not instant. In the first few years, growth looks slow and boring. But over 15–20 years, the curve bends upward sharply. That is why people say starting early matters more than starting with a big amount.

You will see compounding mentioned with FDs, PPF, and mutual fund SIPs. The idea itself is simple: leave money working long enough, and time does a lot of the heavy lifting.

title: Inflation
explanation:
Remember when a movie ticket was ₹120? Today it might be ₹250. That slow, steady rise in prices is inflation — not a scam, just how economies work as things get costlier over time.

Now here is why it matters personally: if your savings account pays 3.5% but prices rise 6% a year, your money is actually going backwards in terms of what it can buy. You have more rupees, but each rupee buys less.

Inflation is why "just keeping money in the bank" feels safe but often is not enough for long-term goals. You do not need to panic — you just need to know it exists so you can plan accordingly.

title: Time value of money
tagline: ₹1 lakh today vs ₹1 lakh in 10 years
explanation:
Your friend owes you ₹10,000. Would you rather get it today, or exactly one year from now? Most people pick today — and not just because waiting is annoying. Money in hand can earn something; money promised later cannot.

Time value of money is the idea that a rupee today is worth more than the same rupee later, because you could put today's rupee to work — in an FD, a mutual fund, or even paying off expensive credit card debt. The longer you wait to receive or invest money, the more future value you give up.

This shows up everywhere: why home loan EMIs feel heavier in year one, why a job offer with delayed joining bonus is weaker than it looks, and why postponing your first investment by five years costs far more than five years of contributions. Delay has a price tag — even when nobody sends you a bill for it.

title: Opportunity cost
tagline: Every choice has a hidden price
explanation:
You chose the ₹450 Swiggy dinner over cooking. Fine — but that is not just ₹450 gone. It is also whatever that ₹450 could have become if it had gone somewhere else.

Opportunity cost is the value of the next best thing you gave up. Every rupee has only one life — spend it on a phone upgrade, and it cannot sit in your emergency fund or chip away at a personal loan. The hidden price of any choice is the future option you closed.

Next time you are about to swipe UPI for something optional, ask: what am I trading this for? Not to kill joy — chai with friends is worth it — but so you spend with open eyes. High earners in Bangalore often feel broke not because they earn little, but because every rupee already has a competing claim.

title: Net worth
tagline: The only number that actually matters
explanation:
Two colleagues both earn ₹18 lakh a year. One owns a flat with ₹40 lakh equity and no credit card balance. The other drives a fancy car on loan and owes ₹12 lakh across cards and a personal loan. On paper their salaries look identical — their actual financial position does not.

Net worth is everything you own minus everything you owe — your flat, FD, mutual fund units, minus home loan, car loan, and that credit card bill you keep rolling. It is the balance sheet of your life, not your monthly salary slip.

Tracking net worth once a year beats obsessing over CTC. A raise that disappears into EMIs does not make you richer. A modest salary with growing assets and shrinking debt does. When relatives ask how you are doing financially, net worth is the honest answer — even if you never say it out loud at family dinners.

title: Cash flow
tagline: Money coming in vs money going out
explanation:
Think of your bank account like a bucket. Salary pours in on the 1st. Rent, EMI, Swiggy, and that auto-debit for Netflix drain it all month. If outflow matches inflow every single month, the bucket never fills — no matter how big the pour.

Cash flow is the rhythm of money coming in versus money going out. Income is only half the story. A ₹2 lakh salary with ₹1.95 lakh in fixed outflows leaves almost nothing to save, invest, or handle surprises.

Positive cash flow — even ₹5,000 a month of surplus — is what actually builds wealth. Check yours once: add up salary and any side income, subtract rent, EMIs, groceries, and subscriptions. The gap is not a moral score. It is the raw material for everything else you want to do with money.

title: Rich vs wealthy
tagline: The difference between being rich and being wealthy
explanation:
The colleague with the imported car and weekend brunches in Indiranagar looks rich. The one who still drives a WagonR but has been quietly investing since 28 might be wealthy — and you would never guess from the parking lot.

Rich usually means high income and visible spending. Wealthy means you have kept and grown what you earned — assets that work even when you sleep. A ₹30 lakh CTC in Mumbai can still mean zero savings if lifestyle expands with every hike.

Chasing the appearance of rich is expensive. Building wealth is often boring: automate savings, avoid bad debt, let investments compound. Nobody posts their net worth on Instagram. That is exactly why the distinction matters for your own choices, not for showing off.

title: Emergency fund
explanation:
Flat tyre on Outer Ring Road at midnight is annoying. Losing your job with ₹800 in the bank and rent due in ten days is a crisis. An emergency fund is the gap between those two feelings.

It is roughly three to six months of essential expenses — rent, groceries, EMIs, insurance — kept where you can reach it quickly: savings account or liquid mutual fund. Not for vacations, not for a phone upgrade. Only for genuine shocks like medical bills, job loss, or family emergencies.

Without this buffer, one bad month pushes you toward credit card debt at 40% interest or selling mutual funds when markets are down. Building even ₹20,000 before chasing higher returns is not timid — it is the foundation everything else stands on.

title: Pay yourself first
explanation:
Most people pay Swiggy, pay the landlord, pay the EMI, and save whatever is left at month-end — which is often zero. Pay yourself first flips that order.

The day salary hits, move a fixed amount to savings or investments before any discretionary spending. What remains in your spending account is genuinely available. You are not relying on leftover willpower after a month of UPI taps.

It works because humans adapt to what they see. If ₹40,000 never lands in your main account, you adjust. Start with an amount that stings slightly but does not break you — even ₹3,000 — and raise it when you get a hike. Future you gets paid like a bill, not a wish.

title: 50-30-20 rule
explanation:
Splitting salary feels overwhelming until someone gives you buckets. The 50-30-20 rule is a starting map: half for needs, thirty for wants, twenty for savings and investments.

Needs are rent, groceries, utilities, school fees — things you cannot skip without serious consequences. Wants are dining out, OTT subscriptions, weekend trips. The twenty percent is your future: emergency fund, FD, mutual funds, extra loan prepayment.

In Bangalore or Mumbai, fifty percent for needs might be a dream — fine, adjust to sixty-forty-twenty or seventy-twenty-ten. The exact ratio matters less than the habit of earmarking something for savings before the month eats everything. Rules are starting points, not exams.

title: Good debt vs bad debt
explanation:
Not all loans are villains. A home loan at 8.5% on a property you will live in for a decade can build an asset. A credit card rollover at 42% annual interest for a gadget you did not need is a wealth destroyer with a friendly EMI label.

Good debt generally funds something that may grow in value or boost earning power — education, a home, sometimes a sensible car for a long commute. Bad debt funds consumption at high rates with nothing left behind except a depreciating object and stress.

Before any EMI, ask two questions: what am I buying, and what is the interest rate? A low-rate home loan and a high-rate card balance are not the same creature. Clearing bad debt often beats chasing investment returns — because no mutual fund reliably beats 40% guaranteed loss.

title: Credit cards
tagline: How to use them without the trap
explanation:
A credit card is essentially a short, interest-free loan from the bank — usually 30 to 45 days — if you pay the full amount on the due date. Used that way, it is convenient for UPI-like tap payments, online bookings, and building a credit history.

The trap opens when you pay only the minimum due. The remaining balance gets charged roughly 36 to 42 percent per year — compounded monthly. One month of rollover can erase a year of careful saving. Rewards points are tiny compared to that interest bill.

Treat the credit limit as a spending cap you never cross, not extra income. Set a calendar reminder for the due date, pay in full, and ignore the bank's suggestion to convert purchases into EMIs unless you have done the math. Discipline here saves lakhs over a decade without any investment skill.

title: Personal loans
explanation:
A personal loan is an unsecured bank loan — no flat or car pledged as collateral — typically at 10 to 18 percent interest. Banks lend based on your salary and CIBIL score, not on whether the expense was wise.

It can make sense for a medical emergency, consolidating expensive credit card debt into one lower EMI, or a time-bound need you genuinely cannot defer. It rarely makes sense for vacations, weddings you cannot afford, or — importantly — investing in stocks or crypto on borrowed money.

Before signing, compare the total interest you will pay over the full tenure, not just the monthly EMI. A ₹5 lakh loan at 14 percent for five years costs far more than ₹5 lakh. If the reason for borrowing does not outlast the EMI, pause and look for alternatives.

title: Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL)
explanation:
That ₹3,000 pair of sneakers split into four payments of ₹750 feels painless — almost like a discount. BNPL apps like LazyPay, Simpl, and pay-in-three at checkout are designed to feel that way.

Buy Now Pay Later is still borrowing. Miss a payment and late fees plus credit score damage follow. Because each purchase feels small, people stack five or six BNPL plans and wonder where the salary went. Free instalments are a marketing trick, not free money.

Use the same test as cash: if you would not buy it outright today, do not BNPL it. One visible subscription in your bank statement beats six invisible instalments scattered across apps. Your future self reconciling the month-end balance will thank you.

title: Credit score
tagline: What it is, why it matters, how to build it
explanation:
When you apply for a home loan, the bank does not just look at your salary. It pulls your CIBIL score — a number between 300 and 900 that summarises how reliably you have repaid debt in the past.

Pay EMIs and credit card bills on time, keep credit utilisation low — using less than thirty percent of your card limit helps — and avoid applying for five loans in one month. Each hard enquiry leaves a small dent. A score above 750 typically unlocks better rates and smoother approvals.

You can check your report free once a year through CIBIL or your bank app. Errors happen — a closed loan still showing open, someone else's default linked to your PAN. Fixing those before you need a loan saves awkward surprises when you are already paying a booking advance on a flat.

title: Saving when everything is expensive
tagline: How to actually save when everything is expensive
explanation:
When rent alone takes forty percent of your salary and onions make headlines, saving can feel like a cruel joke. It is not — but the strategy changes when money is tight.

Start embarrassingly small if you must: ₹1,000 or ₹2,000 a month builds the habit without requiring a lifestyle overhaul. Cut one recurring leak first — the gym membership you never use, the cab when metro works, the third food-delivery app subscription.

Perfection is not the goal. A year of ₹2,000 monthly beats waiting until you earn ₹5 lakh and magically save half. Habits compound like money — the person who saves something every month at ₹8 lakh is better positioned than the one who saves nothing at ₹12 lakh waiting for the perfect moment.

title: Sinking funds
tagline: Saving for a specific future expense
explanation:
Your car insurance renewal arrives every year — same month, predictable amount. Yet it still feels like a surprise expense that wrecks the budget. That is what sinking funds fix.

A sinking fund is money set aside for a known future cost: school fees in June, a cousin's wedding, annual health check-up, or replacing your laptop in two years. Unlike an emergency fund, you know roughly when and how much you need.

Divide the target by months until due and transfer that amount monthly to a separate savings pot or RD. ₹24,000 insurance in twelve months means ₹2,000 a month — boring, automatic, and infinitely less stressful than scrambling in March when the premium message pops up.

title: Automating savings
explanation:
Willpower is unreliable at 11 pm when Zomato sends a notification. Your bank's standing instruction works at 6 am on salary day whether you feel motivated or not.

Automation moves a fixed amount from salary account to savings, RD, or mutual fund SIP on a set date. You decide once; the system repeats. Most people who consistently build wealth are not more disciplined — they just removed themselves from the decision every month.

Set the auto-debit for the day after salary credit, before rent and EMIs drain the account. Start modestly and increase when you get a raise. Money you never see in your spending balance is money you will not accidentally allocate to another sale on Amazon.

title: Why you must invest
explanation:
Keeping everything in a savings account feels safe — until you notice prices climbing faster than your 3.5 percent interest. Inflation quietly shrinks what your rupees buy. Saving alone preserves cash; it does not always preserve purchasing power.

Investing means putting money into assets that can grow faster than prices rise — equity mutual funds, FDs, government schemes, gold. Each carries different risk, but the shared goal is making your money work instead of sitting idle.

You do not need to become a stock picker. Even a simple combination of safe and growth assets beats leaving lakhs in a savings account for ten years. The point is not gambling — it is not letting time and inflation erode the future you are trying to build.

title: Risk vs return
explanation:
Your grandmother's FD feels boring but predictable. Your colleague's equity fund doubled in three years — then dropped fifteen percent in one month. Same country, same rupees, completely different ride.

Higher potential return almost always comes with higher risk — the chance that value falls, sometimes sharply, before it recovers. Savings accounts and government-backed schemes sit at the safe, slow end. Stocks and equity funds sit at the faster, bumpier end.

There is no product that gives equity-like returns with FD-like safety — anyone promising that is selling something. Know your comfort with ups and downs before choosing. A good night's sleep during a market fall is worth more than chasing an extra two percent on paper.

title: Diversification
tagline: Don't bet everything on one thing
explanation:
If all your money sits in one company's stock and that company stumbles, your entire plan stumbles with it. Spreading across different types of investments means one bad outcome does not sink the whole ship.

Diversification is owning a mix — equity, debt, gold, maybe property — so they do not all move the same way at the same time. When stocks fall, debt or gold may hold steadier. Within stocks, owning many companies through an index fund beats betting on one hot tip from the office WhatsApp group.

You are not trying to pick the single best investment. You are building a portfolio where no single failure is fatal. For most salaried Indians starting out, a couple of well-chosen mutual funds across asset types already achieves most of the benefit.

title: Asset classes
tagline: Stocks, bonds, gold, real estate explained
explanation:
Finance people love categorising things. Asset classes are the big buckets: equity means owning pieces of companies, debt means lending to companies or government for interest, gold and real estate are the physical stores of value Indians know well.

Each bucket behaves differently. Equity can soar in good years and sting in bad ones. Debt is steadier but not risk-free — especially corporate bonds. Gold often holds up when markets panic. Property is illiquid but emotionally familiar.

Mixing buckets smooths your journey more than picking one winner. You do not need ten products — understanding these four categories helps you read any recommendation, any news headline, and any relative's advice with clearer eyes.

title: Liquidity
tagline: How quickly can you get your money back
explanation:
Your savings account balance is available at 2 am on a Sunday via UPI — that is highly liquid. Your FD has a lock-in. Your flat in Pune might take six months and brokerage fees to convert to cash — that is illiquid.

Liquidity is how quickly you can turn an investment into spendable money without a big loss. Emergency money must stay liquid. Money for a goal ten years away can sit in less liquid options that may offer better returns.

Before locking funds into a five-year FD or a property down payment, ask: will I need this cash sooner? Trapping money that you might need tomorrow in something that pays well but releases slowly is how people sell investments at the worst time or borrow expensively in a crunch.

title: Rupee cost averaging
tagline: Why timing the market doesn't matter
explanation:
Trying to guess whether the Nifty will be lower next Tuesday is exhausting and usually wrong. Rupee cost averaging sidesteps the guessing entirely.

Invest a fixed amount on a fixed schedule — say every month — regardless of whether markets are up or down. When prices are high, your money buys fewer units. When prices drop, the same rupees buy more. Over time, your average purchase price smooths out the bumps.

That is the mechanical logic behind SIPs, and it works because it removes emotion from timing. You will never buy at the perfect bottom — nobody does consistently. You will, however, avoid the classic mistake of investing only after a long rally when everyone feels brave.

title: SIP
explanation:
A Systematic Investment Plan — SIP — is an auto-debit from your bank into a mutual fund on a chosen date each month. Set it once for ₹3,000 or ₹10,000; the fund buys units at that day's price.

You do not need a lump sum or perfect market timing. SIPs fit salaried life because they match how income arrives — monthly, predictably. The fund house handles the rest; you handle living your life.

Consistency matters more than the amount you start with. Missing months because markets look scary defeats the purpose. Think of SIP as a habit tied to salary day, like rent — except this payment goes to future you.

title: Lump sum vs SIP
explanation:
You just received a ₹5 lakh bonus. Invest it all today, or drip ₹40,000 monthly over a year? Lump sum versus SIP is really a question of when money arrives and how you handle stress.

Lump sum can make sense when you already have a large amount and markets are depressed — you are buying cheap in one shot. SIP makes sense when money comes monthly from salary and you want to avoid the anxiety of picking a single entry date.

Research slightly favours lump sum for long horizons if you invest immediately — but only if you will not panic when markets dip the next week. For most earners, SIP removes that psychological landmine. Choose the method you will actually stick with, not the one that looks optimal on a spreadsheet you will abandon.

title: CAGR
explanation:
A fund statement says your investment grew 80 percent over five years. Sounds huge — but is that 16 percent every year, or something else? CAGR answers that question.

CAGR — Compound Annual Growth Rate — is the smooth yearly rate that would take your starting value to your ending value if growth happened evenly. It accounts for compounding, unlike dividing total gain by years.

If ₹1 lakh became ₹2 lakh in five years, CAGR is about 14.9 percent — not 20 percent. Use CAGR when comparing funds or investments over the same period. It is the honest apples-to-apples number hiding inside confusing absolute returns.

title: Absolute return vs CAGR
explanation:
Your friend brags: my fund is up 60 percent. Over what period — six months or six years? Absolute return tells you total gain; it says nothing about time.

Absolute return is the simple difference: invest ₹1 lakh, it becomes ₹1.5 lakh, that is 50 percent absolute. CAGR spreads that gain across years so you can compare a three-year fund with a ten-year fund fairly.

Apps and agents love quoting big absolute numbers from short hot streaks. Always ask for CAGR over at least five years before comparing. A 40 percent absolute return in one great year is not the same as 12 percent CAGR over a decade — and for long-term goals, the decade number is what actually matters.

title: Power of starting early
explanation:
Two friends invest the same amount monthly into the same fund. One starts at 25, the other waits until 35. At 55, the early starter often has dramatically more — not because they invested longer in a trivial sense, but because compounding had more years to work.

Early contributions get the longest ride. Money invested in your twenties still grows through your thirties, forties, and fifties. Money that starts in your mid-thirties misses that first decade of quiet multiplication — and you cannot buy that time back later with bigger instalments.

Waiting for the perfect salary, the perfect market, or the perfect fund is expensive. Starting small now beats starting large later for most long-term goals. The best month to begin was last year; the second best is this salary cycle.

title: Setting financial goals
explanation:
Save more is not a goal — it is a wish without a deadline. Save ₹25 lakh for a home down payment by March 2029 is a goal. Your brain and your bank app can actually work with the second one.

Good financial goals have a rupee amount, a timeline, and a name you care about — child's college, parent's medical buffer, your own sabbatical. Vague intentions leak money to Swiggy and sales; specific targets get automatic transfers.

Once you have the number and date, work backwards. How much monthly into an FD, debt fund, or equity SIP gets you there given reasonable return assumptions? Adjust the timeline or the monthly amount until it fits your cash flow. A goal you can execute beats a dream you only discuss at chai.

title: What is a mutual fund
explanation:
Think of a mutual fund like a potluck dinner. Everyone brings a little money — maybe ₹500, maybe ₹5,000 — and a professional chef (the fund manager) decides what to cook with it. Instead of buying shares of Reliance or HDFC Bank yourself, you buy units of the fund that holds many companies at once.

The company running the fund is called an AMC (Asset Management Company) — think HDFC Mutual Fund or SBI Mutual Fund. They charge a small annual fee for managing your money. Your share of the pot is measured in units, and the price of one unit is called NAV (Net Asset Value), which changes daily based on how the underlying investments perform.

Why bother pooling? Two reasons: you get diversification even with small amounts, and you do not need to track 30 stocks yourself. For most salaried Indians opening their first investment app, a mutual fund is the entry point — not because it is fancy, but because it is practical.

title: How mutual funds make money
tagline: How a mutual fund actually makes you money
explanation:
You make money from a mutual fund in two main ways. First, when the stocks or bonds inside the fund go up in value, your units become worth more — that is capital appreciation. Second, some funds pay out dividends (from company profits) or interest (from bonds), which either land in your bank account or get reinvested automatically.

The number you watch is NAV — Net Asset Value, the per-unit price. If you bought units at ₹50 and NAV rises to ₹65, your investment has grown. When you need the money, you redeem (sell back) your units at the current NAV. The fund house credits your bank account, usually within 2–3 working days for most equity funds.

What eats into returns? Expense ratio (annual management fee), exit load if you leave too early, and taxes on gains when you sell. The fund itself does not guarantee returns — if markets fall, your NAV falls too. That is normal, not a scam.

title: NAV
tagline: What it is and what it isn't
explanation:
NAV stands for Net Asset Value — basically the price tag on one unit of a mutual fund. The fund house adds up everything it owns (stocks, bonds, cash), subtracts what it owes, divides by total units, and publishes that number every evening after markets close.

Here is the trap beginners fall into: thinking a fund with NAV ₹15 is "cheaper" than one at ₹150. That is like saying a ₹15 pizza slice is cheaper than a ₹150 whole pizza without checking the size. NAV only tells you the current unit price — it says nothing about whether the fund will grow well from here.

What actually matters is the fund's track record over 5–10 years, its expense ratio, and whether the category fits your goal. A fund that went from ₹10 to ₹100 NAV over a decade is a winner; a fund stuck at ₹15 for five years is not, regardless of how "affordable" it looks today.

title: Expense ratio
explanation:
Every mutual fund charges an annual fee for running the show — salaries, research, marketing, compliance. That fee, expressed as a percentage of your investment, is the expense ratio. A 1.5% expense ratio means ₹1,500 per year on a ₹1 lakh investment gets deducted quietly from the fund's returns.

Active funds — where a manager picks stocks — typically charge 1–2%. Index funds that simply mirror Nifty 50 might charge 0.1–0.3%. The difference sounds tiny, but over 20 years it compounds into a serious gap. Two identical funds returning 12% gross, one at 0.3% expense and one at 1.5%, can leave you with lakhs less at the end.

Where to find it: the fund's fact sheet or the AMFI website. Before investing, always check this number. It is the one cost you can control without needing to predict the market.

title: Exit load
explanation:
Exit load is a penalty fee the fund charges if you pull your money out too soon. For many equity funds, redeeming within one year costs you 1% of the amount withdrawn. On a ₹2 lakh redemption, that is ₹2,000 gone — not to the market, but to the fund house as a deterrent against short-term trading.

Why do funds do this? Churning — people jumping in and out — forces the manager to buy and sell frequently, hurting returns for long-term investors. Exit load protects patient holders. Debt and liquid funds often have lower or zero exit load, but always check the scheme document.

Practical takeaway: match your fund choice to your timeline. If you might need the money within a year, a liquid fund or FD makes more sense than an equity fund with exit load. Plan to hold equity funds at least 3–5 years, and exit load becomes a non-issue.

title: Direct vs regular plan
explanation:
When you buy a mutual fund, you pick a plan type — Direct or Regular. Same fund, same manager, same stocks inside. The difference is how you buy it. Direct means you go straight to the AMC website or apps like Groww, Zerodha Coin, or Kuvera. Regular means you buy through a distributor or agent who gets a commission.

That commission is not billed separately — it is baked into a higher expense ratio on the Regular plan. Over 15 years, Direct plans typically return 0.5–1% more annually because you skip the middleman's cut. On a growing portfolio, that gap becomes substantial.

If you are comfortable choosing funds yourself (or following a simple index fund strategy), Direct is the obvious choice. Regular plans made sense when the internet did not exist and agents actually advised you. Today, for most informed investors, Direct wins on cost alone.

title: Equity vs debt funds
explanation:
Equity funds put your money mostly in stocks — shares of companies listed on NSE and BSE. When those companies do well, your fund grows; when markets crash, your fund drops. Higher ups and downs, but historically better long-term returns. Good for goals 5+ years away: retirement, child's college, wealth building.

Debt funds put your money in bonds — essentially loans to the government or companies that pay fixed interest. Much steadier ride, lower returns than equity. Think of them as a smarter cousin of FDs: not guaranteed, but usually less volatile. Good for goals 1–3 years away: house down payment, car, tax planning.

Many beginners pick equity because it sounds exciting, then panic when markets fall 15%. Match the fund type to your timeline and stomach for volatility. A 25-year-old saving for retirement can handle equity swings; someone saving for a wedding next year should lean debt.

title: Index funds
explanation:
An index fund does not try to beat the market — it simply copies it. A Nifty 50 index fund buys the same 50 large companies that the Nifty index tracks, in the same proportions. No fund manager making bold bets on which stock will soar. Just quiet, mechanical tracking.

Why would you want something so boring? Because most active fund managers fail to beat their benchmark index over 10 years, especially after fees. The Nifty itself has delivered roughly 12% annualised over long periods. An index fund captures that return minus a tiny fee — often under 0.2%.

Warren Buffett famously bet that a simple index fund would beat fancy hedge funds over a decade — and won. For most Indians who do not want to spend weekends analysing funds, a Nifty index fund as a core holding is hard to argue against.

title: ELSS
tagline: The fund that saves tax too
explanation:
ELSS stands for Equity Linked Savings Scheme — a mutual fund category that comes with a tax benefit. Invest up to ₹1.5 lakh per year and claim a deduction under Section 80C, reducing your taxable income. The catch: your money is locked for three years. No early withdrawal, no exceptions.

Because ELSS invests in equities, returns can be bumpy but potentially rewarding over the lock-in period. It is one of the few tax-saving options that gives you equity exposure — unlike PPF or NSC which are pure debt. Many salaried Indians use ELSS as their primary 80C instrument.

One caution: do not invest in ELSS only for the tax break if you cannot lock money for three years. A tax saved today means nothing if you are forced to borrow at 18% interest because your money is stuck. Treat it as a long-term equity investment that happens to save tax, not the other way around.

title: Large cap vs mid cap vs small cap
explanation:
Companies on the stock market are grouped by size — measured by market cap (total value of all shares). Large-cap means big, established names: Reliance, TCS, HDFC Bank. They are slower but steadier — like the senior managers of the corporate world.

Mid-cap companies sit in the middle — growing fast but not yet giants. Think of successful regional brands or niche leaders. Small-cap companies are the smallest listed firms — high growth potential, but one bad quarter can halve the stock price. SEBI defines these buckets: top 100 companies are large-cap, 101–250 mid-cap, 251+ small-cap.

Large-cap funds suit conservative investors who want equity exposure without wild swings. Mid and small-cap funds can deliver higher returns in good years but fall harder in bad ones. If a fund's category makes you nervous during a 20% market drop, you probably picked too aggressive a cap size for your comfort.

title: SIP in a falling market
explanation:
Markets fall — sometimes 10%, sometimes 30%. Headlines scream crisis, WhatsApp groups share panic, and your mutual fund app shows red numbers. This is when most people stop their SIP (Systematic Investment Plan), which is exactly the wrong move.

Here is why continuing helps: your SIP buys a fixed rupee amount every month. When NAV is high, you get fewer units. When NAV drops, the same ₹5,000 buys more units. Over time, your average purchase price smooths out — you accumulate more units during cheap periods.

Think of it like buying dal at the kirana store. If the price drops this month, would you stop buying dal? No — you would stock up. A falling market is a sale for long-term SIP investors. The only people who lose in crashes are those who sell, not those who keep buying steadily.

title: How to pick a mutual fund
explanation:
There are thousands of mutual funds in India. Picking one feels overwhelming, but you do not need to analyse all of them. Start with three filters: does the category match my goal timeline? Is the expense ratio reasonable? Has the fund performed consistently over 5–10 years, not just last year?

Check the fund manager's tenure — a good track record means little if the manager who built it left six months ago. Compare returns against the benchmark (Nifty for large-cap, etc.), not against other random funds. A fund beating its benchmark by 1–2% consistently is doing its job.

Avoid chasing last year's top performer — that fund often attracted so much new money it becomes harder to manage. Also skip funds you cannot understand from the fact sheet. When in doubt, a low-cost Nifty index fund beats most active picks for beginners. Boring is fine when you are building a foundation.

title: How to read a mutual fund fact sheet
tagline: What to look for on the fact sheet
explanation:
Every mutual fund publishes a monthly fact sheet — a free PDF on the AMC website or AMFI portal. It is the fund's report card: what it owns, how it performed, and what it costs. Spend ten minutes on it before investing a single rupee.

Key sections to scan: Top holdings (which companies or bonds the fund owns), sector allocation (how much in banking, IT, pharma, etc.), expense ratio, and performance vs benchmark over 1, 3, 5, and 10 years. If the fund holds 40% in one sector you are uncomfortable with, that is useful to know upfront.

Red flags: a brand-new fund with no track record, expense ratio above 2% for an index-like strategy, or performance that wildly swings year to year. If the fact sheet confuses you even after a careful read, that fund might be too complex for your needs — a simple index fund is a perfectly respectable choice.

title: KYC and PAN
tagline: What you need to start investing
explanation:
Before you buy your first mutual fund or open a demat account, SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) requires you to complete KYC — Know Your Customer. It is a one-time identity verification: your PAN card, Aadhaar, a photo, and bank account proof. Standard anti-fraud stuff.

PAN (Permanent Account Number) is mandatory for all investments in India — the 10-character ID on your PAN card. Without it, no fund house will accept your money. e-KYC through apps like CAMS, KFintech, or your broker takes under ten minutes and works across most platforms once done.

Keep your KYC updated if you change your address or phone number. An outdated KYC can block redemptions when you actually need the money. Do this once, do it right, and you never think about it again.

title: AMFI and SEBI
explanation:
Two names show up whenever mutual funds are discussed: SEBI and AMFI. SEBI is the government regulator — it makes the rules, approves new funds, and can penalise AMCs that misbehave. Think of SEBI as the traffic police for India's investment highways.

AMFI (Association of Mutual Funds in India) is the industry body — it represents fund houses, sets operational standards, and runs the AMFI website where you can look up any registered fund. AMFI does not regulate; SEBI does. But AMFI's resources are useful for investors checking if a scheme is legitimate.

Your money in a SEBI-registered mutual fund is held by a separate custodian bank, not by the AMC itself. Even if the fund company goes bankrupt, your units are safe. This separation is a key reason mutual funds are considered safer than giving money to random investment schemes.

title: PPF
explanation:
PPF — Public Provident Fund — is a 15-year savings account backed by the Government of India. You can open one at any post office or major bank. The interest rate is set by the government every quarter — recently around 7–7.5% — and the entire maturity amount is tax-free.

You can deposit between ₹500 and ₹1.5 lakh per year. Deposits qualify for Section 80C tax deduction. After 15 years, you can extend in blocks of 5 years or withdraw. Partial withdrawals are allowed from year 7 onwards. It is one of the safest long-term instruments in India — no market risk, no company risk.

PPF suits conservative investors building a retirement cushion or parents saving for a child's future. The 15-year lock-in is long, so do not put money you might need for a house down payment in three years. But for slow, steady, tax-free wealth building, PPF remains a solid pillar.

title: EPF
tagline: The money your employer adds every month
explanation:
If you are a salaried employee in India, EPF (Employee Provident Fund) is probably already running without you noticing. Every month, 12% of your basic salary goes into EPF, and your employer matches another 12%. That is 24% of your basic — forced retirement savings you did not have to opt into.

The money earns interest set by the EPFO (Employees' Provident Fund Organisation), currently around 8%+. It is tax-free on withdrawal after five continuous years of service. Your UAN (Universal Account Number) tracks the account across job changes — check your passbook on the EPFO portal or UMANG app.

EPF is not optional for most private-sector jobs, and that is actually a good thing. Many people discover a substantial corpus only when they check after five years. Do not withdraw it when switching jobs unless you absolutely must — transfer it to the new employer and let it compound quietly.

title: VPF
tagline: Voluntarily adding more to your EPF
explanation:
VPF — Voluntary Provident Fund — is exactly what it sounds like: you choose to put extra money into your EPF beyond the mandatory 12%. There is no separate account. The extra contribution sits in the same EPF pot and earns the same government-set interest rate.

Why bother? If you have already maxed your PPF at ₹1.5 lakh and still want safe, tax-efficient savings, VPF is an attractive option while you are employed. The interest is tax-free on withdrawal after five years, same as regular EPF. No market volatility, no fund selection headache.

The catch: VPF only works while you have an active EPF account through an employer. If you quit, go freelance, or retire, you cannot add new VPF contributions. It is a useful tool for salaried people in their peak earning years who want more safe debt in their portfolio.

title: NPS
tagline: Retirement savings with a tax benefit
explanation:
NPS — National Pension System — is a long-term retirement account regulated by PFRDA. You contribute regularly (or lump sum), choose how to split between equity and debt, and build a corpus for age 60 and beyond. It offers an extra tax deduction of ₹50,000 under Section 80CCD(1B), over and above the ₹1.5 lakh 80C limit.

At retirement (age 60), you must use at least 40% of the corpus to buy an annuity — a product that pays you monthly pension for life. The remaining 60% can be withdrawn as lump sum (partially tax-free). You cannot touch the money freely before 60, with few exceptions.

NPS makes sense if you are disciplined about retirement and want the extra ₹50,000 tax break. It is not for short-term goals or emergency money. Equity exposure within NPS is capped, so returns may lag a direct mutual fund SIP — but the forced discipline and tax benefit have their own value.

title: Sovereign Gold Bonds
explanation:
Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) are issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India. Instead of buying physical gold jewellery or coins, you buy a bond whose value tracks the gold price. You get gold price appreciation plus 2.5% annual interest paid twice a year — no making charges, no locker, no purity anxiety.

Each bond has an eight-year tenure, with exit options from year five onward. If you hold till maturity, capital gains are completely tax-free — a benefit physical gold and gold ETFs do not offer. You can buy during RBI tranches through banks, post offices, or stockbrokers. There is a per-person limit each year.

SGBs are the most tax-efficient way to hold gold for investment purposes in India. They are not for trading — liquidity on the stock exchange can be thin. Buy with a long-term view, the way you would buy gold for a child's wedding 10 years out, not to flip next month.

title: NSC
explanation:
NSC — National Savings Certificate — is a five-year fixed deposit sold at post offices across India. You invest a lump sum, earn a fixed interest rate set by the government (currently around 7%), and get your principal plus interest back at maturity. Simple, no-frills, government-backed.

Deposits qualify for Section 80C tax deduction up to ₹1.5 lakh. Here is a twist: the interest earned each year is taxable, but it is treated as reinvested — so you can claim it as 80C deduction in subsequent years too (within the ₹1.5 lakh cap). Your post office passbook tracks everything.

NSC suits conservative savers who want a fixed return without market risk and prefer the familiar post office over apps. The five-year lock-in is shorter than PPF's 15 years. Returns are modest and fully taxable at maturity, so it works best for those in lower tax brackets or who have already filled their 80C with EPF and ELSS.

title: Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana
explanation:
Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY) is a government scheme for a girl child below 10 years of age. Open an account at a post office or bank with her birth certificate. Deposits earn a high interest rate (recently 8%+) that is completely tax-free, and contributions qualify for 80C deduction up to ₹1.5 lakh per year.

The account runs until the girl turns 21, with partial withdrawal allowed at 18 for education or marriage expenses. Minimum deposit is ₹250 per year — even small amounts keep the account active. Only one SSY account per girl child, maximum two accounts per family (for two daughters).

If you have a young daughter and want a safe, tax-free corpus for her education or future, SSY is among the best options in India. The long tenure matches a child's timeline perfectly. Just remember: the money is locked for years, so do not put funds you might need for your own emergencies.

title: PM Vaya Vandana Yojana
explanation:
PM Vaya Vandana Yojana (PMVVY) is a pension scheme for Indian citizens aged 60 and above, administered by LIC. You invest a lump sum — up to ₹15 lakh — and receive a guaranteed monthly pension for 10 years. The pension rate is set at launch and does not change.

It is designed for retirees who want predictable monthly income without worrying about market ups and downs. The returns are modest — often in the 7% range — and the pension is taxable as income. After 10 years, you get your principal back.

PMVVY makes sense for seniors who prioritise certainty over growth. It will not beat inflation over a decade, so it works best as one pillar of retirement income alongside other sources like EPF, rental income, or a senior citizen FD — not as the only plan.

title: RBI Floating Rate Bonds
explanation:
RBI Floating Rate Savings Bonds are government-backed bonds where the interest rate adjusts every six months based on the NSC (National Savings Certificate) rate plus a small spread. When government small-savings rates go up, your bond interest goes up too — hence "floating rate."

You invest a minimum of ₹1,000 with no upper cap. Interest is paid twice a year directly to your bank account. The tenure is seven years with no early exit — your money is locked for the full period. Interest is fully taxable at your income slab rate.

These bonds suit conservative investors who want better returns than a savings account and prefer government safety over corporate bonds or debt funds. Buy through designated banks when the RBI opens a subscription window. They are not tradable on the stock exchange, so plan to hold till maturity.

title: Fixed Deposit
tagline: How it works, when to use it
explanation:
A Fixed Deposit (FD) is the simplest investment most Indians know — you give a lump sum to a bank for a fixed period (7 days to 10 years), and the bank pays you a guaranteed interest rate. SBI, HDFC, ICICI, your local cooperative bank — all offer FDs. The rate is locked at booking and does not change even if market rates move.

Major bank FDs currently offer roughly 6–7.5% depending on tenure. Senior citizens get an extra 0.25–0.5%. Interest above ₹40,000 per year (₹50,000 for seniors) from one bank branch attracts TDS — tax deducted at source — unless you submit Form 15G/15H.

Use FDs for money you need back within 1–3 years with certainty: a house down payment, school fees, or an emergency buffer beyond your savings account. FDs will not beat inflation over long periods, but for short, predictable goals they still do the job reliably.

title: Recurring Deposit
explanation:
A Recurring Deposit (RD) is like an FD but you deposit a fixed amount every month instead of one lump sum. Your bank or post office deducts ₹2,000 or ₹5,000 (whatever you choose) on a set date, and at the end of the tenure — typically 1–5 years — you get the total with interest.

Interest rates are similar to FDs of the same tenure. The math is straightforward: you know exactly how much you will receive at maturity when you start. Post office RDs are popular in smaller towns; most bank apps let you set one up in minutes.

RDs are good for disciplined saving toward a specific goal — a vacation, festival expenses, or a gadget purchase next year. They are not exciting and will not make you rich, but they build the habit of regular saving without any market risk. Think of them as a structured piggy bank with interest.

title: Debt mutual funds
explanation:
Debt mutual funds invest your money in bonds — government securities, corporate debentures, treasury bills — rather than stocks. A fund manager pools money from many investors and buys a diversified basket of debt instruments. You buy units, same as an equity fund, but the underlying assets are loans, not company shares.

Returns come from interest payments and changes in bond prices. They are not guaranteed like an FD — if interest rates rise sharply, bond prices fall and your NAV dips temporarily. But over short periods, quality debt funds are much steadier than equity funds and often deliver better post-tax returns than FDs for those in the 20–30% tax bracket.

Choose the right sub-category for your timeline: liquid funds for under 3 months, ultra-short duration for 3–6 months, short duration for 1–3 years. Do not treat debt funds as identical to FDs — they carry some interest-rate risk and credit risk. Read the portfolio before investing.

title: Liquid funds
explanation:
Liquid funds are a type of debt mutual fund that invests in very short-term instruments — treasury bills, commercial paper maturing within 91 days. Because the loans inside mature quickly, the fund's value barely fluctuates. Redemption usually hits your bank account next business day.

Returns are modest — typically 4–7% depending on RBI rates — but consistently better than leaving large sums idle in a savings account earning 3–3.5%. If you have ₹2 lakh sitting in your bank after receiving a bonus, parking it in a liquid fund until you decide what to do with it is smarter than letting it sleep.

Use liquid funds for your emergency fund (beyond the immediate cash you keep in savings), for parking money between investments, or for any need within a few weeks to months. They are low-risk but not zero-risk — stick to funds from reputable AMCs with clean credit histories.

title: Corporate bonds
explanation:
When you buy a corporate bond, you are lending money to a company. The company pays you regular interest (called the coupon) and returns your principal at maturity. Higher-rated companies like AAA-rated Tata or L&T pay lower interest because they are safer bets. Lower-rated companies offer higher yields to compensate for higher default risk.

You can buy corporate bonds on the NSE/BSE bond platform or through bond-focused apps. Minimum investment varies — some start at ₹10,000, others at ₹1 lakh. Unlike FDs, there is no deposit insurance. If the company goes bankrupt, you may lose part or all of your money.

Never chase a 12% yield when FDs offer 7% without asking why. Check the credit rating from agencies like CRISIL, ICRA, or CARE. A AA-rated bond paying 8.5% might be reasonable; a BBB-rated bond paying 12% is a gamble dressed as an investment.

title: Government securities (G-Secs)
explanation:
Government securities — G-Secs or gilts — are bonds issued by the Government of India to fund its spending. When you buy a G-Sec, you are lending to the most creditworthy borrower in the country. The sovereign guarantee means default risk is essentially zero.

Until recently, retail investors needed lakhs to buy G-Secs directly. RBI Retail Direct (rbiretaildirect.org.in) changed that — you can open a free account and buy government bonds with as little as ₹10,000. Alternatively, gilt mutual funds let you invest smaller amounts and leave the buying to a fund manager.

G-Secs offer lower returns than corporate bonds because they are safer. They suit conservative investors who want maximum safety and can hold for 5–10 years. Interest is taxable, and bond prices fall when rates rise — so even "risk-free" does not mean "price-stable" in the short term.

title: Bond ratings
tagline: How to know if a bond is safe
explanation:
Credit rating agencies — CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, and others — evaluate how likely a company or bond issuer is to repay its debt. They assign grades from AAA (safest, highest quality) down through AA, A, BBB, and all the way to D (default). Think of it as a report card for borrowers.

Higher rating means lower interest offered — investors accept less because they trust repayment. Lower rating means higher yield — the company must pay more to attract lenders willing to take the risk. When you see a bond offering 11% and FDs offer 7%, the rating tells you where that extra 4% comes from: risk.

As a rule, stick to AA or AAA for conservative portfolios. BBB and below are for investors who genuinely understand default risk and can absorb losses. If an agent pushes a "guaranteed 12%" bond without mentioning the rating, that is your cue to walk away and check independently.

title: What is a stock
tagline: Owning a piece of a company
explanation:
When you buy a stock, you buy a tiny slice of a real company — like owning one brick in a Reliance tower, except your brick is electronic and lives in a demat account. If the company grows profits over years, more people want that slice, and the price can rise.

Companies list on NSE or BSE so they can raise money from the public instead of only from banks. As a shareholder, you may get dividends when they share profits, and you can vote on some big decisions — though most small investors never bother with the voting part.

Stocks are not a salary replacement or a lottery ticket. They are ownership in businesses that sell phones, run banks, or ship exports. That is why prices wobble daily but long-term returns often track how well the business actually performs.

Many Indians start with mutual funds, which bundle many stocks together. Direct stock picking is the same idea — ownership — just concentrated in one or a few companies, with more research and more emotional swings along the way.

title: IPO explained
explanation:
An IPO is a company's debut on the stock market — the first time ordinary investors can buy its shares through NSE or BSE. Before that, only early investors, promoters, and private funds could own it.

You apply through your broker or bank app during the IPO window, often paying via UPI. If demand is huge, you may get only a partial allotment or none at all — oversubscribed IPOs are common when the brand is famous.

Not every IPO is a bargain. Some list at high prices and fall within months; others like certain tech listings have done well. Read the prospectus for revenue, debt, and how the company will use the money — not just the logo and celebrity ads.

Think of an IPO as buying a flat in a new building on day one. The brochure looks glossy, but you still want to check the builder's track record, location, and whether the price makes sense before signing.

title: Demat account
tagline: What it is and how to open one
explanation:
A demat account holds your shares in electronic form — no paper certificates, no locker anxiety. When you buy HDFC Bank or a Nifty ETF, the units sit in this account, linked to your PAN, just like salary sits in your bank account.

You open one through a SEBI-registered broker: Zerodha, Groww, ICICI Direct, and others. The process is mostly online — PAN, Aadhaar e-sign, bank proof, and a short video KYC. Many people finish in under fifteen minutes on a lunch break.

Your broker gives you a trading account to place buy and sell orders; the demat account is where the shares actually land. Two accounts, one login — confusing at first, normal after your first purchase.

There is no minimum balance required to keep a demat account open, but some brokers charge annual maintenance if you are inactive. If you only invest via mutual funds, you may not need a demat at all — but for direct stocks and ETFs, you do.

title: NSE vs BSE
explanation:
India has two main stock exchanges: NSE (National Stock Exchange) in Mumbai and BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange), one of the oldest in Asia. Most large companies list on both, so Reliance trades on NSE and BSE with the same ISIN code.

NSE handles more daily volume for many names; BSE has a longer history and its own index, the Sensex. For you as a retail investor, the exchange matters less than the broker's platform fees and the stock itself.

Nifty 50 tracks the top 50 stocks on NSE; Sensex tracks 30 on BSE. When TV says "market is up 500 points," they usually mean one of these indices — shorthand for how big Indian companies did that day.

Pick a broker you trust and understand. Whether your Infosys shares settle via NSE or BSE will not change your returns — liquidity and your buy price matter far more than the exchange badge.

title: Nifty 50 and Sensex
explanation:
Nifty 50 and Sensex are scoreboards for the Indian stock market — baskets of the largest, most traded companies. When Nifty rises 1%, it roughly means those 50 giants moved up together on average, not that every stock in India did.

They are weighted by company size, so Reliance or HDFC Bank moves the index more than a smaller name in the basket. That is why Nifty can look healthy while your mid-cap portfolio is flat — you are looking at different slices of the market.

You cannot buy Nifty directly, but you can buy a Nifty index fund or ETF and own a tiny piece of all 50 companies in one go. It is the lazy, diversified way to bet on India Inc without picking individual stocks.

Daily index moves make headlines, but your SIP does not need today's number. Over ten or fifteen years, what matters is whether Indian companies as a group grew earnings — the index is a rough mirror of that story.

title: Market cap
explanation:
Market cap is the total price tag the stock market puts on a company — share price multiplied by total shares outstanding. If TCS trades at ₹4,000 and has about 365 crore shares, its market cap runs into many lakh crores.

SEBI groups companies into large-cap (top 100), mid-cap (101–250), and small-cap (rest). Large caps like ITC or HUL tend to be steadier; small caps can double fast or halve in a bad quarter — more excitement, more stomach-churning.

Market cap is not the same as "good company." A hot small stock can have a tiny cap but wild speculation; a boring large cap may grow slowly for decades. Size tells you how the stock typically behaves, not whether you should buy it.

Mutual fund categories use the same labels — large-cap funds, mid-cap funds. Matching the cap size to your risk appetite and time horizon matters more than chasing whichever bucket did best last year.

title: How stock prices move
explanation:
Stock prices change every second during market hours because buyers and sellers agree on a new price — pure supply and demand. Good quarterly results can attract buyers; a scandal or global panic can send sellers rushing for the exit.

In the short run, prices can look irrational — a rumour on Twitter, a foreign fund selling, or nothing obvious at all. That daily noise is why checking your portfolio every hour is exhausting and usually pointless.

Over years, profits, revenue growth, and management quality tend to pull prices toward reality. A company earning more per share year after year often sees its stock follow, even if the path is bumpy.

Think of it like house prices in your locality. Today's quote might reflect one desperate seller or a bidding war; the long-term trend still ties to the area's jobs, infrastructure, and demand — fundamentals, not just mood.

title: How to read a stock
tagline: PE ratio, EPS, book value basics
explanation:
Before buying a stock, glance at a few numbers — not to become an analyst overnight, but to avoid obvious traps. P/E ratio compares the share price to annual profit per share; a very high P/E can mean high hopes or overpricing.

EPS (earnings per share) tells you how much profit the company made for each share — rising EPS over years is a healthy sign. Book value is assets minus liabilities per share; useful for banks and old industrial companies, less so for asset-light tech firms.

Never use one ratio alone. A low P/E might mean a bargain or a company in trouble. Compare to peers in the same industry — a pharma stock's P/E should be read against other pharma names, not against a bank.

If the numbers confuse you, that is fine — stick to index funds until you enjoy reading quarterly results. Stock picking without basic literacy is like buying a flat without seeing the floor plan.

title: Dividends
explanation:
Some companies share a portion of profits with shareholders as cash dividends — credited straight to your bank account linked to the demat. ITC, Coal India, and many public-sector firms are known for regular payouts.

Dividend yield is the annual dividend divided by the share price — a ₹10 dividend on a ₹200 stock is 5% yield. High yield can mean generous sharing or a falling share price making the yield look artificially large.

Young growth companies like many tech startups often pay zero dividends — they reinvest profits to expand. Mature, cash-rich businesses pay out because they have more money than growth projects need.

For most wealth building, price growth plus reinvested dividends beat chasing the highest yield alone. A 2% yield from a company growing fast can outperform a 6% yield from a business slowly shrinking.

title: Stock splits and bonuses
explanation:
A stock split cuts the share price and gives you more shares — a 1:2 split turns one ₹1,000 share into two ₹500 shares. Your total value stays the same; it just feels cheaper, which sometimes attracts more retail buyers.

Bonus shares are free extra shares issued from accumulated profits — a 1:1 bonus doubles your share count at zero cost to you. Again, total value does not magically jump on announcement day; the price adjusts downward proportionally.

Neither split nor bonus creates new wealth by itself. They are accounting and psychology tools — splits improve liquidity; bonuses reward loyal shareholders without cash outflow from the company.

Do not buy a stock just because a split or bonus is coming. If the business is weak, extra shares at half the price still leave you with a weak investment.

title: How to buy your first stock
explanation:
Your first stock purchase is mostly paperwork you have already done — demat open, bank linked, funds added. During market hours (9:15 am to 3:30 pm IST), search the company symbol on your broker app and place a market or limit order.

Start with one large-cap name you understand — something whose product you use — or a Nifty 50 index ETF if picking feels scary. Buy a small quantity; the goal is learning the flow, not doubling your money in a week.

Avoid F&O, penny stocks, and tips from WhatsApp groups for your first year. Those are advanced tools and traps dressed as shortcuts — most beginners lose money there while thinking they are investing.

After you buy, you will see red and green daily. That is normal. Your first stock is a classroom fee for understanding ownership, taxes, and your own panic reflex — keep the amount small enough that a 20% drop does not ruin your sleep.

title: How to research a company
explanation:
Research starts with a simple question: what does this company sell, and who pays for it? If you cannot explain it to a friend over chai, pause before buying — complexity hides risk.

Check the last four quarters of results on BSE or Moneycontrol — revenue and profit trending up is a green flag; rising debt with falling margins is a worry. Promoter holding above 50% often means founders still care; heavy promoter pledge can signal stress.

Compare valuation to two or three competitors. If every bank stock trades at 15x earnings and yours is at 40x, ask why — maybe justified, maybe hype. Read the management commentary in the annual report for honest context, not just the headline numbers.

You do not need a CFA to do basic homework — thirty minutes per company beats blind tips. If that feels like work, a Nifty index fund does the research for you by owning the whole basket.

title: Annual reports
explanation:
Every listed company publishes an annual report once a year — a thick PDF with audited numbers, chairman's letter, and risks the company admits might hurt them. It is free on the company website or BSE/NSE portals.

Focus on three sections: profit and loss (are sales and margins growing?), balance sheet (how much debt versus cash?), and cash flow (is profit turning into real cash or just paper?). Auditors' notes flag issues in plain-ish language if you scroll far enough.

Skip the glossy photos; read the fine print on related-party transactions and contingent liabilities — legal cases, tax disputes, loans to promoter entities. Surprises often hide there, not in the press release.

You do not need to read 200 pages for every stock. Even skimming ten pages of a company you own beats never opening the report at all — it is the closest thing to looking under the hood before a long drive.

title: Promoter holding
explanation:
Promoters are founders and their families — the people who built or control the company. Promoter holding is the percentage of shares they still own. When founders keep a large stake, their wealth rises and falls with yours.

SEBI requires quarterly shareholding pattern disclosures. Watch for slow promoter selling over many quarters — not always bad, but worth asking why. Pledged shares (promoters using stock as loan collateral) are a red flag when pledge levels climb above 50% of their holding.

High promoter holding does not guarantee honesty — frauds have happened with promoters still in charge. But very low holding with a newly listed company sometimes means insiders cashed out at the IPO and you are holding the bag.

Check this once when you buy and again every few months if it is a large position for you. Five minutes on the BSE filing page can save you from riding a stock where the people who know it best are quietly exiting.

title: ESOPs and RSUs
tagline: Equity pay for salaried tech workers
explanation:
If you work at a startup or large IT firm, part of your pay may come as ESOPs (options to buy company shares later at a fixed price) or RSUs (shares granted outright after a vesting period). Flipkart, Infosys, and hundreds of others use these.

Vesting means you earn the right over time — leave before four years and you forfeit unvested units. Exercise price on ESOPs is what you pay to convert options to shares; if the market price is below that, the options are underwater and worthless for now.

Paper wealth is not cash until you sell — and tax hits on exercise or sale depending on structure. Many Bangalore engineers have seen lakhs on screen disappear when the company stalled or the market corrected before they sold.

Treat ESOPs as a bonus, not your emergency fund. Diversify outside your employer — if the company struggles, you lose salary and stock together. That concentration risk is real even when the grant letter looks generous.

title: Why Indians trust gold
explanation:
Gold runs through Indian life — wedding muhurats, Akshaya Tritiya queues at Tanishq, grandmother's bangles passed down as inheritance. That cultural trust did not appear overnight; centuries of stability when other assets failed built it.

Financially, gold has held value when the rupee weakens or when stock markets panic — 2008, 2020, and many rupee dips saw gold demand spike. It is a hedge, not a growth engine; prices creep up but rarely compound like equity over twenty years.

Trusting gold emotionally is fine; treating all your savings as jewellery is not. Making charges on ornaments eat 10–20% the day you buy; you pay again when you sell. Separate emotional gold from investment gold in your head.

Modern India offers SGBs, ETFs, and digital gold for the financial role without the locker. Tradition and smart allocation can coexist — one thali for the heart, a small SGB tranche for the portfolio.

title: Physical gold vs digital gold
explanation:
Physical gold means coins, bars, or jewellery you can touch — bought from a jeweller or bank. Purity certificates help, but making charges on jewellery mean you lose value instantly; a ₹50,000 chain may sell back as ₹42,000 scrap gold.

Digital gold on apps like Paytm or PhonePe lets you buy fractions of a gram stored in vaults — no locker, no theft worry at home. Spreads between buy and sell prices can be 3–5%, and not all apps offer easy withdrawal as physical bars.

For wearing at a wedding, physical gold wins. For pure investment, both physical and digital lose to Sovereign Gold Bonds or gold ETFs on cost, tax, and transparency — fewer middlemen taking a cut.

If you already own heavy jewellery, count that toward your gold allocation before buying more digitally. Many Indian households are overweight gold without realising it because ornaments are never marked to market.

title: Sovereign Gold Bonds
tagline: The best way to own gold
explanation:
Sovereign Gold Bonds are issued by the RBI — you lend money to the government and get gold price exposure plus 2.5% interest paid twice a year. No making charges, no purity doubt, no locker rental.

Buy during RBI tranches through your bank or demat account; each person has an annual limit. Hold till eight-year maturity and capital gains on the gold portion are tax-free — a sweet deal you do not get on jewellery or most ETFs.

You can exit early on the exchange after the fifth year, but then tax treatment changes. For long-term gold allocation in a portfolio, hold-to-maturity SGBs are hard to beat on a spreadsheet.

They are illiquid between tranches and the limit caps how much you can add per year — plan tranche by tranche rather than expecting to dump ₹20 lakh in one shot. Patience fits gold's role anyway: slow, steady, defensive.

title: Gold ETFs
tagline: Stock market way to buy gold
explanation:
A gold ETF trades on NSE like a stock — each unit backed by roughly one gram of gold stored in a vault. Buy through your demat account during market hours; sell the same way when you need cash.

Expense ratios are low compared to digital gold apps — often around 0.5% or less. You pay brokerage on trades and demat charges, but no making charges or wastage.

ETFs suit tactical allocation — you want 5% gold in your portfolio and rebalance yearly. They are less ideal for rupee-cost averaging tiny amounts because each buy needs a demat and a minimum lot size on some brokers.

Tax on sale follows gold rules — LTCG if held long enough, STCG if sold sooner. Unlike SGBs at maturity, there is no tax-free exit on ETFs alone — factor that into SGB versus ETF choice for long holds.

title: Gold mutual funds
explanation:
Gold mutual funds invest in gold ETFs or physical gold on your behalf — you buy units from the AMC without opening a demat. SIP of ₹500 or ₹1,000 monthly is easy on Groww, Coin, or fund house apps.

They are slightly more expensive than holding the ETF directly because of the fund layer, but the convenience of SIP and no demat hassle suits many salaried investors building gold slowly.

Use them to diversify alongside equity SIPs — same auto-debit date, same habit, different asset class. When Nifty falls, your gold SIP may be the part of the portfolio that holds steady.

Check whether the fund buys ETF units or physical gold; either works, but expense ratio should stay under 1%. Above that, you are paying a lot for convenience you might get cheaper elsewhere.

title: Gold in a crisis
explanation:
When COVID crashed markets in March 2020 or during global scares, gold often rose while Nifty bled — investors flee to something that feels permanent. That is the hedge role: not to make you rich, but to cushion the fall.

Gold does not always rise in every bad week — it is not a perfect inverse of stocks. But over decades, a small gold slice has reduced portfolio swings for many Indian investors who panic-sell equity at the bottom.

During a crisis, headlines push gold ads hard — jewellers, apps, everyone sells fear. Stick to your allocation plan; doubling gold after it already spiked is chasing, not hedging.

Five to ten percent in gold means a ₹10 lakh portfolio has ₹50,000–₹1 lakh there — enough to matter psychologically when equity is red, not enough to drag long-term growth if held for decades.

title: Gold allocation
tagline: How much gold should you hold
explanation:
Most financial planners suggest 5–10% of your investable wealth in gold — not 50%, not zero unless you have family jewellery that already counts. The exact number matters less than having a deliberate choice instead of accidental overload.

If your mother already gifted heavy wedding gold, you may need little extra in SGBs or ETFs — mark jewellery at approximate value and add only to fill a gap. Urban renters with no physical gold might lean toward the upper end of the range.

Rebalance once a year — if gold runs up and becomes 15% of your portfolio, skim a little into equity or debt to restore balance. Gold's job is stability, not hero returns.

Gold will not fund your retirement alone at 7% inflation and children's fees. Treat it as insurance in the asset mix, with equity doing the heavy wealth lifting over fifteen-plus years.

title: Renting vs buying
explanation:
The rent-versus-buy debate in India is emotional because "own house" equals success in family conversations. Run the numbers anyway — in Bangalore or Mumbai, rent for a 2BHK might be ₹25,000 while EMI for a similar flat crosses ₹60,000 after a ₹30 lakh down payment.

Buying wins when you plan to stay seven to ten years, EMI is close to rent, and you have stable income for maintenance, society charges, and property tax. Renting plus investing the difference in mutual funds has beaten buying in many Indian cities over the last decade on pure math.

Opportunity cost is the silent killer — ₹20 lakh down payment at 12% equity returns grows to over ₹61 lakh in ten years. That future wealth does not show up in the broker's home-loan pitch.

Neither choice is morally better. Renting is not "throwing money away" if you invest the surplus; buying is not always building wealth if EMI chokes your SIP and the flat appreciates slowly. Match the decision to your city, tenure, and cash flow — not uncle's opinion at Sunday lunch.

title: How real estate generates returns
tagline: How real estate actually generates returns
explanation:
Real estate makes money two ways: price going up and rent coming in. Indian dinner-party stories focus on doubling in five years; spreadsheets after stamp duty, brokerage, maintenance, and vacant months often show 5–8% annualised — decent, not magical.

Rental yield in most Indian cities is low — 2–3% of property value per year in many metros. A ₹1 crore flat earning ₹25,000 rent is normal; most return comes from hoping the next buyer pays more, not from rent cash flow.

Under-construction promises, builder delays, and legal title issues eat returns you never see on the brochure. A "20% discount pre-launch" means nothing if possession slips three years and you pay rent plus EMI together.

Track net return after all costs, not gross stories. If you would not accept 6% from a mutual fund with lock-in and legal risk, ask why 6% from property feels exciting — often it is familiarity bias, not superior maths.

title: REITs
tagline: Owning real estate without buying property
explanation:
REITs let you buy units of commercial buildings — offices, malls, warehouses — on the stock exchange without ₹5 crore for a whole floor. Like a mutual fund, but the underlying assets are rent-earning properties managed by professionals.

Listed REITs on NSE pay out most rental income as dividends — Embassy, Mindspace, and others have made this accessible to ordinary demat holders. You get liquidity that physical property lacks; sell units in minutes during market hours.

Prices still fluctuate with interest rates and office vacancy — COVID hurt commercial REITs when work-from-home emptied towers. Dividends are taxable; yields vary with property quality and lease renewals.

REITs suit investors who want property exposure without EMIs, society meetings, or tenant calls at midnight. They are a slice of a portfolio, not a replacement for your first home decision.

title: InvITs
tagline: Infrastructure without buying a toll road
explanation:
InvITs (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) are cousins of REITs — instead of office rent, you earn from highways, power transmission lines, or gas pipelines. Tolls and tariffs flow to unit holders as dividends after maintenance and debt costs.

Listed InvITs like IRB or PowerGrid-linked structures trade on NSE with lower entry than buying a toll road yourself. Yields can look attractive at 8–12%, but depend on traffic growth, regulatory tariff resets, and how much debt the trust carries.

Infrastructure is long-life but politically and operationally messy — a highway with falling traffic or a delayed tariff revision hits distributions. Read the trust's asset list and debt levels before chasing yield.

Treat InvITs as income-oriented satellite holdings for experienced investors who already have equity and debt covered. They are not beginner instruments, but they open a door to assets your neighbour cannot literally show you at a housewarming.

title: Home loan basics
explanation:
A home loan is a long marriage with a bank — you borrow crores, repay in EMIs over 15–20 years, and the house is collateral until you clear the loan. Rate, tenure, and loan amount together fix your monthly EMI; online calculators spell it out in seconds.

A ₹50 lakh loan at 8.5% for twenty years means roughly ₹43,000 per month. In early years, most of that EMI is interest, not principal — depressing but normal. A ₹1 lakh prepayment in year two saves more interest than the same ₹1 lakh in year fifteen.

Floating rates move with RBI policy; fixed-rate offers are rare and often reset anyway. Budget for registration, stamp duty, GST on under-construction, modular kitchen, and society deposit on top of down payment — the EMI is not the full cost.

Banks approve based on salary, credit score, and property papers. Get a sanction letter before falling in love with a flat; sellers and builders take you seriously when the bank already said yes up to a limit.

title: Prepaying a home loan
explanation:
Prepayment means paying extra toward principal before the schedule — a bonus, inheritance, or deliberate savings chunk. Every rupee of prepayment reduces future interest on the remaining balance; there is no smarter use of prepayment than early in the loan.

When home loan rates were 9% and equity returned 12% long term, maths favoured investing the lump sum instead of prepaying. When rates hit 8.5% and markets are expensive, prepaying a guaranteed 8.5% saving wins for risk-averse minds.

Some banks charge prepayment penalties on fixed legacy loans; most floating-rate home loans allow partial prepayment freely — confirm in your loan agreement. Keep six months' expenses in emergency fund before dumping every bonus into the loan.

Psychological peace matters too. A debt-free home by 45 feels different from maximum spreadsheet optimisation. Run both numbers — optimal and comfortable — and pick the one you will stick with without regret.

title: Commercial vs residential
explanation:
Residential property — flats and houses — is what most Indians buy first. Rental yields are often 2–3% in metros; you bet mainly on price appreciation and personal use, not monthly rent covering EMI.

Commercial — shops, offices, warehouses — can yield 8–10% rent but needs bigger ticket sizes, longer vacancy gaps, and understanding lease law. A shop in a tier-2 high street differs wildly from a vacant office in a new SEZ.

Banks lend more easily on residential; commercial loans have shorter tenure and higher rates. REITs offer commercial exposure without those hurdles for small investors.

Do not assume commercial is "better" because yield sounds higher — vacancy, tenant defaults, and cyclical downturns hurt commercial harder. Residential is simpler; commercial is a business, not just a roof.

title: Real estate risks
explanation:
Property is illiquid — selling a flat in Pune can take six months of broker visits, negotiations, and buyer loan approvals. You cannot sell three bedrooms on a bad Monday like you redeem a mutual fund.
